title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
oneLineScope: How a token gathers information from other tokens via weighted soft lookup — the core operation of the transformer.
prose:
Where we are. The last few nodes were all building toward this one. Word embeddings gave us a vector for each word — but a fixed one, so “bank” gets the same vector in “river bank” and “savings bank.” The RNN/LSTM baseline could in principle use context to tell those apart, but it had to push the entire history through one hidden state, one step at a time. Then alignment and attention showed the way out, in machine translation: instead of compressing everything into a single vector, let each position reach back and take a weighted look at all the others. This node takes that idea — soft, learned alignment — and distills it into the one operation the whole transformer is built from. It is worth slowing down here; almost everything later is a variation on what happens in this node.

The gist, in one paragraph. Scaled dot-product attention is a recipe that lets every position in a sequence build its own custom summary of the whole sequence. Each position looks at every other position, scores how relevant each one is to it right now, turns those scores into weights that add up to one, and takes the weighted average of what those positions have to offer. Nothing is hard-selected; everything is blended, in proportion to relevance. And because the scores are computed from the representations themselves, and every step is differentiable, the network learns what “relevant” ought to mean for the task.

Why it matters. This is the heart of the machine. Multi-head attention is just several of these running in parallel; the transformer block wraps one in standard plumbing; the full transformer stacks those blocks. Understand this operation and the rest of the architecture is largely assembly. It is also the clean break from recurrence: every position reaches every other one directly, in a single parallel step, with no fixed-width bottleneck and no waiting for the previous timestep to finish.

The idea: a soft lookup

The cleanest mental model is a soft dictionary lookup. An ordinary lookup — a hash map, a database index — matches a query against stored keys and returns the one value whose key matches exactly. That is a hard, discrete operation, and it has no useful derivative, so it cannot sit inside a network you train by gradient descent. Attention is its smooth relaxation: instead of demanding an exact match and returning one value, it scores the query against every key, turns those scores into a probability distribution, and returns the weighted average of all the values — each value weighted by how well its key matched.

Make it concrete with a sentence the model is reading: “The cat didn't cross the road because it was too tired.” To represent it well, this position needs to figure out what it refers to. With attention, the it position issues a query that, in effect, asks “which earlier word am I standing in for?” It compares that query against every other position and finds that cat answers it far better than road. So the new representation of it becomes mostly a copy of what cat has to offer, with a little of everything else mixed in. No rule told it to do this; the comparison fell out of the learned representations.

If you know the statistical alignment models from machine translation — the IBM models, or HMM-based word alignment — you already know the shape of this idea. There, a latent alignment variable decides which source word a target word comes from, and EM gives you a soft posterior over alignments. Attention is that same move made differentiable and learned end to end: the alignment weights are computed on the fly from the representations, not estimated as a separate latent-variable model, and gradients flow straight through them. The alignment and attention node traces that lineage; here we take the operation as Vaswani et al. published it and pin down its mechanics.

Queries, keys, and values

To make the lookup work, each position emits three vectors, all simple learned linear projections of its current representation:

  • a query — “what am I looking for?”
  • a key — “what do I offer to others who might look at me?”
  • a value — “what do I actually hand over if I am attended to?”

Splitting the key from the value is the quietly important design choice. The key decides whether a position gets attended to; the value decides what is delivered when it does. A token can advertise itself one way and carry a payload of a different character, and the two roles are trained independently. The projections being learned is what lets the same word play different roles in different sentences: through the loss, the network discovers which directions of the representation should drive matching (the query/key space) and which should be passed along as content (the value space).

The operation, with dimensions

Now the formalism — which should feel like a transcription of what we just described. Let the input be \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), with one row per position (\(n\) positions, each a vector of width \(d_{\text{model}}\)). Three learned weight matrices produce the queries, keys, and values:

\[ Q = X W_Q,\quad K = X W_K,\quad V = X W_V \]

with \(W_Q, W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}\) and \(W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}\), so that \(Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}\). The whole operation is then one line:

\[ \operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V \]

Read it left to right by shape, and it is exactly the soft lookup. \(Q K^{\top}\) is \(n \times n\): entry \((i, j)\) is the dot product of query \(i\) with key \(j\) — one raw relevance score for every (looker, looked-at) pair. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) rescales those scores (more on that next). The \(\operatorname{softmax}\) runs row by row, so each row turns into a probability distribution that sums to one: row \(i\) is the set of weights position \(i\) places on every position. Call that matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\). Finally \(A V\) is \(n \times d_v\): each output row is the weighted average of all the value vectors, using that row's weights. One position in, one context-aware vector out — computed for all \(n\) positions at once, in a single pair of matrix multiplies.

It helps to put numbers to the shapes once. Take a short sequence of \(n = 10\) tokens with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) and \(d_k = d_v = 64\). Then \(Q, K, V\) are each \(10 \times 64\); the score matrix \(Q K^{\top}\) is \(10 \times 10\) (one hundred query–key comparisons); after scaling and the row-wise softmax, \(A\) is still \(10 \times 10\) with each row summing to one; and \(A V\) is \(10 \times 64\) — ten context vectors, one per position, each a blend of the ten value vectors. Keep your eye on that \(n \times n\) score matrix: it is where “who looks at whom” lives, and every later variant of attention is, at bottom, a different way of shaping it.

Why divide by √d_k

This is the detail people skip and then misremember, so here it is carefully. If the query and key entries are roughly independent with zero mean and unit variance, their dot product over \(d_k\) dimensions has variance on the order of \(d_k\), so its typical size grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Feed scores of that magnitude into a softmax and it saturates: almost all the weight collapses onto the single largest score, the distribution becomes nearly one-hot, and the gradient through the softmax goes flat — and it gets worse at larger \(d_k\), exactly where you hoped for more capacity. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalizes the score variance back to order one, keeping the softmax in its responsive range regardless of head size. It is a variance-control trick, not a deep identity; the full argument is the footnote in §3.2.1 of Vaswani et al.

Masking: reading only what you should

As written, every position can see every other, which is correct for an encoder reading a complete input at once. Two situations require hiding specific entries, and both do it the same way — by setting the offending scores to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so the exponential sends their weight to exactly zero. The first is the causal mask: for generating text left to right, predicting token \(t\) from tokens \(1\ldots t{-}1\), a position must not peek at its own future, so every score \((i,j)\) with \(j > i\) is masked out. This is the hinge the autoregressive language modeling node turns on. The second is the padding mask: when sequences of different lengths are batched and padded to a common length, the padding positions are masked so no real token attends to filler. Same mechanism, different bookkeeping.

What it costs, and where it leads

The score matrix is \(n \times n\), so both compute and memory grow as \(O(n^2 d)\) in the sequence length. For the modest \(n\) of this era that is cheap, and — crucially — it is parallel: every score is independent, so the whole thing is two big matrix multiplies a GPU does at once, in a constant number of steps rather than the \(n\) sequential steps an RNN must take. That short, fixed path between any two positions is what finally made long-range dependencies learnable. (The same quadratic term is what later long-context work spends its effort attacking, but that is a frontier-era concern, out of scope here.) With this single operation in hand, two doors open immediately: running several of these in parallel on different learned subspaces (multi-head attention), and confronting the fact that, because attention is a sum over an unordered set, nothing here yet knows the order of the tokens — the gap that positional encoding exists to fill.

diagrams.caption: Data flow of scaled dot-product attention for a single head, with every tensor shape labeled.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline. Input matrix X (n by d_model) projects via W_Q, W_K, W_V into Q (n by d_k), K (n by d_k), and V (n by d_v). Q and K feed a matrix multiply producing the score matrix Q-K-transpose (n by n), which is divided by the square root of d_k and passed through a row-wise softmax to give the attention weight matrix A (n by n). A and V feed a final matrix multiply producing the output (n by d_v). A note marks that a causal mask sets above-diagonal scores to minus infinity before the softmax.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram, left to right, of scaled dot-product attention for a single head. On the left, an input matrix labeled X with shape n by d_model, drawn as a short stack of rows to suggest n positions. Three arrows labeled '× W_Q', '× W_K', and '× W_V' lead from X to three matrices: Q (shape n by d_k), K (shape n by d_k), and V (shape n by d_v). Q and K feed a matrix-multiply box that produces a score matrix labeled 'Q Kᵀ' with shape n by n; emphasize this scores matrix as the heart of the operation. An arrow labeled '÷ √d_k' leads from the scores into a box labeled 'softmax (row-wise)', annotated with the note 'each row sums to 1', producing the attention weight matrix labeled A with shape n by n. A and V feed a final matrix-multiply box producing the output matrix with shape n by d_v on the right. Label every matrix with its name and its shape. Add a small margin note with a leader line at the scores matrix reading: 'causal mask: set entries above the diagonal to −∞ before softmax'. Structural diagram: shapes and flow must be exact.

diagrams.caption: The soft-lookup intuition: a query blends all values in proportion to how well it matches each key.
diagrams.altText: A single query card on the left reading 'what am I looking for?' connects to a row of several key cards each reading 'what I offer', and behind each key sits a value card. Bands of varying thickness run from the query to each key, suggesting a soft weighted match across all of them rather than selecting one. The result on the right is shown as a blend of the values weighted by match strength.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual analogy illustration of attention as a 'soft lookup'. On the left, a single query drawn as a small labeled card reading 'what am I looking for?'. In the middle, a row of several key cards each reading 'what I offer', and behind or beside each key card a matching value card carrying a small payload. Draw bands of varying thickness from the single query to each key, the thicker bands meaning a stronger match; emphasize that the query connects to ALL keys at once with different strengths rather than picking exactly one. On the right, show the result as a blended value — a mixture of the value cards combined in proportion to the match strengths. No equations and no tensor shapes; this is the plain-language intuition companion to the structural diagram. Conceptual analogy: vibe over precise labels.

expansion: Deeper treatment the prose deliberately omits, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the full variance argument for √d_k scaling, including the independence/unit-variance assumptions and what breaks when they fail; (2) the comparison to additive (Bahdanau) attention and why the dot-product form wins on speed despite similar quality at small d_k — Vaswani §3.2.1; (3) complexity analysis O(n²·d) in time and memory, and the path-length / parallelism argument from §4 that motivates attention over recurrence; (4) the precise softmax-gradient saturation analysis. Cite each claim to its source section; do not introduce results from outside the bibliography.
